newsitem.title: USA: Crews try to restore power before new Pacific storm.
newsitem.headline: Crews try to restore power before new Pacific storm.

text.p: Hundreds of utility crews scrambled on Saturday to restore power to tens of thousands of customers in Washington state and Oregon before another Pacific storm slams the region with snow, rain and bursts of fierce wind.
Snow and freezing rain on Thursday and Friday left more than 170,000 homes and businesses in the western states without electricity, down from nearly 300,000 on Friday.
The powerful storm ruined holiday travel plans for thousands, stranding motorists on icy roads and grounded and delayed flights from San Diego to Seattle.
Utility crews raced against time on Saturday to reconnect homes and repair power lines while the region's weather was relatively calm before the next storm.
"They're trying to restore as much power as they possibly can before this new storm moves in," Betty Werblun, a spokeswoman for Puget Sound Power and Light Co. said.

Puget Power, which services nine counties in western Washington state, said 140,000 of its customers were still without power. Puget Power said 120 of its repair crews were working around the clock to restore electricity. Repair crews from Canada were brought in to help, but she said snow and ice made their work slow and difficult.
"They will work as hard and as fast as they can," Werblun said. "But potentially, the incoming storm could undo what we've already done."

In Oregon, about 29,000 Portland General Electric Co. customers remained without electricity following Thursday's ice storm. "It's a mess out there," Portland General Electric spokeswoman Vickie Rocker said.
She said 200 crews would work through the weekend to restore power to homes, but warned the changing weather could hamper their efforts.
The new Pacific storm, carrying snow, rain and powerful winds, was expected to strike the region later on Saturday.

Freezing rain and snow was forecast for Oregon and Washington. A winter storm watch was declared in the Portland area, which could see one to two inches (5.1 cm) of snow on Saturday before the snow turns into freezing rain. Widespread flooding was reported in northwest Oregon.

A winter storm warning was in effect for much of Washington state. Southwest Washington was expected to see freezing rain mixed with snow. By late on Sunday, the Seattle area northward could receive four to 10 inches (10 to 25 cm) of new snow.
Meanwhile, severe winds and rain were forecast for central and northern California. Emergency personnel were preparing for disaster -- floods, mudslides and widespread power outages.

The storm could dump more than 10 inches (25 cm) of rain and cause major flooding in parts of northern and central California, forecasters said. Heavy rains were expected in the Santa Cruz Mountains and along California's Russian River.

Thousands of people living close to the Russian River were preparing for the worst, said Chris Godley, assistant coordinator of the Sonoma County emergency services department. Some residents on rivers and streams were stacking sandbags to protect their homes.
Rain from the storm could melt snow in lower mountain areas of California, adding to the potential for dangerous flooding further inland, forecasters said.

In northern California, winds could reach 35 to 45 mph (56 to 72 kph) with gusts to 60 mph (96 kph) in lower elevations, and wind bursts to well over 100 mph (161 kph) over the highest ridges of the Sierra Nevada.
"This is a major storm," said National Weather Service forecaster Bob Benjamin, based in Monterey, California. "We're going to get pounded."
